title: iPhone 18 Pro Could Cost $300 More as Memory Chip Shortage Drives 38% Build Cost Surge
excerpt: AI data center demand has sent DRAM and NAND prices soaring, pushing Apple's component costs up 38% and setting the stage for the biggest iPhone price hike in years.
body:
• The iPhone 18 Pro could start at $1,399, up $300 from the current iPhone 17 Pro, as Apple faces a 38% increase in component costs driven by surging memory chip prices.
  • Memory now accounts for roughly 34% of iPhone component costs, up from 10% a year ago, as AI data center demand creates a global DRAM and NAND shortage.
  • Apple CEO Tim Cook called the memory price surge "a hundred-year flood," and the company has already raised prices on Macs, iPads, Apple TV, HomePod, and Vision Pro.
  • Apple may absorb part of the increase by switching to its own C2 modem and cutting non-memory component costs, potentially limiting the consumer-facing hike to $50-$100.

Apple's next iPhone lineup will cost significantly more to build, and consumers will feel at least part of the impact. Multiple analyst reports now estimate that the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials will rise 38% over its predecessor, with soaring memory chip prices responsible for the bulk of the increase.

The Memory Math

According to TrendForce's latest analysis, memory accounted for about 10% of the iPhone Pro's total component cost a year ago. That figure is projected to reach 34% in the third quarter of 2026 and exceed 40% by early 2027. The shift is dramatic enough that memory has displaced the display as the single most expensive component in the device.

https://x.com/iPhoneinCanada/status/2091568952480571703

TechInsights estimates that Apple paid roughly $39 for the 12GB of DRAM in the iPhone 17 Pro — a cost that could climb to $145 for the iPhone 18 Pro. The 256GB flash storage tier, which cost Apple about $13 last year, could rise to $51. Combined with non-memory components estimated at $530, the total bill of materials for the base iPhone 18 Pro would reach approximately $726, up from $582, according to The Wall Street Journal.

J.P. Morgan's own analysis projects the iPhone memory bill rising from $65 in 2025 to $114 in 2026 and $228 in 2027, tracking a five- to sevenfold increase in memory prices since the start of 2025.

Why Chips Are So Expensive

The culprit is a global shortage of DRAM and NAND flash storage driven by the rapid buildout of AI data centers. Manufacturers including Samsung Electronics and Micron Technology have shifted production toward enterprise-scale memory chips for AI servers, squeezing supply for consumer electronics.

"The consumer electronics industry is facing an unprecedented challenge. The rapid expansion of AI data centers has created an extraordinary surge in demand for memory and storage. We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly."

— Apple official statement

Apple CEO Tim Cook has described the situation as "a hundred-year flood on the memory pricing" and acknowledged that price increases were "unavoidable." The company already raised prices across 14 products in June, including every Mac and iPad model, the Apple TV, HomePod, and Vision Pro. The iPhone lineup was spared in that round, but analysts expect it to be next.

How Much More Will You Pay?

Analyst Jeff Pu of GF Securities estimates the iPhone 18 Pro could start at $1,399 and the iPhone 18 Pro Max at $1,499 — increases of up to $300 over current pricing. The 1TB iPhone 18 Pro Max faces the steepest component cost increase, with Counterpoint Research estimating NAND flash costs alone exceeding $250 for that model.

However, the consumer-facing increase may be more modest. J.P. Morgan estimates that non-memory component costs could fall from $449 to $426 this year, partly offsetting the memory surge. Apple's expected shift from Qualcomm to its own C2 modem in the iPhone 18 Pro could save an additional $15. Digital Trends reports that the practical price increase may land between $50 and $100 rather than the full $300 some analysts have projected, if Apple chooses to absorb part of the cost increase.

What's Coming in September

Apple is expected to announce the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and its first foldable iPhone next month. The iPhone 18 Pro will reportedly feature a 2nm A20 Pro chip manufactured on TSMC's N2 process — itself carrying a premium over the current 3nm node — along with a variable-aperture main camera. TrendForce expects Android vendors in the entry-level and mid-range segments to raise prices even more steeply than Apple, or to drop product lines entirely.
